cases.title: The Great Fire of London
cases.description: What caused this fire, and how did London recover?

questions.body: You've just arrived at a bakery that appears to be the mysterious origin point of a terrifying blaze engulfing London. Observing the scene, you identify the owner of this bakery as your first key witness. Where exactly did this devastating fire begin its deadly spread?
questions.answer: Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane
questions.original: Where did the Great Fire of London start?

questions.body: As you examine the destroyed neighborhood, the true cause of the rapid fire's spread becomes clear. What factor in the construction of these buildings allowed the fire to race through the streets so quickly?
questions.original: What was the main reason the fire spread so rapidly?

questions.body: Investigating further, you note the relentless duration of this disaster. How many days did the Great Fire continue to burn before it was finally brought under control?
questions.original: How many days did the Great Fire burn?

questions.body: Walking through the ashes, you count the ruins where homes once stood. How many houses were destroyed in this catastrophic firestorm?
questions.original: Approximately how many houses were destroyed?

questions.body: Among the many buildings lost to the fire, one stands out as a major cultural symbol that was completely destroyed. Which famous London church was consumed by the flames?
questions.original: Which famous church was destroyed in the fire?

questions.body: Examining the records and speaking with survivors, you learn about the human cost of the fire. How many people are officially recorded as having died in this tragic event?
questions.original: How many people are officially recorded as having died in the Great Fire?

questions.body: To fight the spreading inferno, firefighters employed a certain risky strategy: creating firebreaks by tearing down buildings to halt the flames. What was this firefighting method primarily used during the Great Fire?
questions.original: What method was primarily used to fight the fire?

questions.body: After the ashes settled, a renowned architect was tasked with a monumental job to rebuild the devastated city. Who was commissioned to oversee the reconstruction of much of London, including key landmarks?
questions.original: Who was commissioned to rebuild much of London after the fire?

questions.body: In your investigation, you come across a valuable personal diary that reveals vivid details about the fire, providing a rare first-hand perspective. Who is the author of this most famous diary account of the Great Fire?
questions.original: Who kept the most famous diary account of the Great Fire?

questions.body: Finally, to piece together the timeline of this disaster, you must determine the exact year when this great calamity struck London. In what year did the Great Fire of London occur?
questions.original: In what year did the Great Fire of London occur?

briefs.body: The Great Fire of London started in a bakery located on Pudding Lane in central London shortly after midnight on September 2, 1666. The fire quickly spread through the city because many of the buildings were made of wood and were built very close to one another, allowing flames to race rapidly across the streets.
briefs.topic: The Great Fire of London Origins and Spread

briefs.body: The fire burned for about four days before it was finally brought under control. Over 13,000 houses and numerous buildings were destroyed in the conflagration, drastically transforming the City of London’s medieval landscape.
briefs.topic: Duration and Impact of the Fire

briefs.body: Among the buildings lost in the fire was St. Paul's Cathedral, an important cultural and architectural landmark. Despite the widespread destruction, the officially recorded death toll was relatively low, with only six people recorded as having died in the disaster.
briefs.topic: Key Buildings Destroyed and Human Cost

briefs.body: The main firefighting strategy during the Great Fire was creating firebreaks, which involved demolishing buildings to stop the fire from spreading further. This method was risky and was not deployed immediately but was crucial in eventually halting the flames.

After the fire, Christopher Wren, a renowned architect, was appointed to oversee the reconstruction of many parts of London, including St. Paul's Cathedral. The firsthand diary of Samuel Pepys provides a detailed account of the fire, offering valuable personal insights into the events and efforts to control the disaster.
The Great Fire of London took place in the year 1666 and is a significant historical event remembered for its dramatic impact on the city, shaping London’s development and history going forward.
